title: An English Pilgrimage: the Allgäu Silence, the Suffolk Coast, and the Road near Poringland
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Wertach im Allgäu, the birth in the father's absence
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Winfried Georg Sebald is born in a Bavarian alpine village, second of three children of Rosa and Georg Sebald. His father joined the Reichswehr in 1929 and went into Poland with the Wehrmacht in 1939; he is a prisoner of war in France on the day of the birth and will not come home for three years. The house belongs to the women and to the grandfather, Josef Egelhofer, a village policeman who walks the boy along the Wertach and names the weather for him. The war ends a year after the birth. Nobody in the valley will describe it to him.
stops.quote: Where I grew up, in a remote village at the back of a valley, the old still thought the dead needed attending to - a notion so universal, it's enscribed in all religions.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Sebald in an English-language interview, circulated on quotation aggregators; primary transcript not traced [R]. Aggregator text reads 'enscribed'; reproduced verbatim.
suggested_refs: The birth house at Grüntenseestrasse 3, Wertach, now the terminus of the Sebaldweg
sources: Carole Angier, Speak, Silence: In Search of W.G. Sebald (2021)

stops.name: Wertach im Allgäu, the father comes back from captivity
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only; no month is given in reachable sources, so the day defaults to 1 January
stops.campa: Georg Sebald returns from French captivity to a son of three who has never lived with him. He takes work again and does not discuss the years in uniform or what the army he served did in Poland. The grandfather remains the boy's real company; the father is a man at the table. Sebald will later describe his parents as small-peasant and farm-labouring people who made the grade during the fascist years. He is not lied to about any of it. He is simply not told.
stops.quote: My parents came from working-class, small-peasant, farm-labourer backgrounds and had made the grade during the fascist years; my father came out of the army as a captain.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Sebald in an English-language interview, circulated on quotation aggregators; primary transcript not traced [R]
suggested_refs: Josef Egelhofer, the maternal grandfather, principal adult of Sebald's first years

stops.name: Sonthofen, the town with the Ordensburg on its edge
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period 1948-1963 (ages four to nineteen); the month of the move is not recorded and defaults to January
stops.campa: The family moves to Sonthofen, where the boy lives from the age of four until he is nineteen. On the edge of the town stands an Ordensburg, one of the castles built to train the Nazi elite, and a population that does not discuss what the buildings were for. Sebald grows up among adults who talk about weather, work and money. No revelation ever arrives. What he has instead is a childhood spent inside an agreed omission, in a landscape that looks as though nothing has happened in it.
stops.quote: Until I was 16 or 17, I had heard practically nothing about the history that preceded 1945.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Sebald in an English-language interview, circulated on quotation aggregators; primary transcript not traced [R]
suggested_refs: The Ordensburg Sonthofen, NS training academy, on the edge of Sebald's childhood town

stops.name: Immenstadt, the Realgymnasium Maria Stern
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by de.wikipedia ('ab 1954'); month defaulted. Coordinates are the centre of Immenstadt im Allgäu, not the school building, which reachable sources do not locate
stops.campa: From the age of ten Sebald attends the Realgymnasium Maria Stern at Immenstadt, down the valley from Sonthofen: Latin, French, the long schoolboy journey, an education conducted as though the century began in 1945. The West German curriculum of the Adenauer years teaches the classics and steps around the recent dead. He reads early and on his own account. In the rooms he sits in, what matters most is the thing no adult present will name, and he is learning to listen for it.
suggested_refs: The Realgymnasium Maria Stern, Immenstadt, Sebald's school from 1954

stops.name: Oberstdorf, the film shown without a word
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed range c. 1961-1963; English Wikipedia gives no year at all, the widely repeated date of 1957 is impossible since Sebald was then still at Immenstadt, and his own interview accounts place the screening in his upper-school years at about seventeen. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: At the Oberrealschule in Oberstdorf a teacher runs film of the liberated camps for the class and offers no word before it and none after. The reel ends, the lights come up, the lesson continues. Sebald is about seventeen. He returns to the moment for the rest of his life, and what he describes is never the footage: it is the silence in the room afterwards, boys and master alike agreeing without discussion that nothing has been shown. He takes his Abitur here in 1963 and leaves the Allgäu.
suggested_refs: The Oberrealschule Oberstdorf, where Sebald sat his Abitur in 1963

segments.name: Leaving the Country, Keeping the Language

stops.name: Freiburg im Breisgau, the faculty that steps around it
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1963-1965; the month is the conventional start of the German winter semester and is not separately documented
stops.campa: Sebald reads German and English literature at Freiburg, in a faculty staffed by men whose careers began before 1945 and whose lectures pass over it. He finds the university a larger version of the family table. He takes a refusal out of the faculty rather than a training. He will not spend his life inside German letters, and he will not write the kind of novel the Federal Republic is producing about itself. The decision to leave the country is made in these lecture rooms, several years before he acts on it.
stops.quote: I hate [...] the German postwar novel like pestilence
stops.quote_source: Interview quotation as reproduced in the English Wikipedia article 'W. G. Sebald'; primary interview and date not traced
suggested_refs: The Albert-Ludwigs-Universität Freiburg, German faculty of the early 1960s

stops.name: Fribourg, the degree taken across the language border
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction [R]: sources agree he studied at both Freiburg and Fribourg but divide the degrees differently; the completion at Fribourg is tagged reconstruction in the research pool. Month defaulted
stops.campa: He crosses into French-speaking Switzerland and finishes his degree at Fribourg, a bilingual town sitting on the language frontier. The displacement is small and he will repeat it at a greater distance. German stays the working language of his mind while the street outside speaks something else, and he will live inside that arrangement for the next thirty-five years. He is twenty-one. He has no intention of returning to Bavaria except as a visitor, and no plan yet for what he intends instead.
suggested_refs: The Université de Fribourg, bilingual campus on the Röstigraben

stops.name: Manchester, a German in the city his countrymen bombed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month not recorded and defaulted
stops.campa: Sebald takes a lectureship in German at the University of Manchester and meets an England coming apart: mills stopped, warehouses black with a century of soot, empty streets around a shrunken quarter whose Jewish families came out of Germany a generation before him. He is a German teaching the bombers' language to English undergraduates in a city his countrymen burned. He walks it constantly, at night, without company. Twenty-five years later these streets carry the story of the painter Max Ferber.
suggested_refs: The University of Manchester German department, Sebald's first English post

stops.name: St Gallen, the year at the Institut auf dem Rosenberg
stops.date_confidence: attested that a St Gallen interlude took place around 1969 (English Wikipedia records a year of school teaching; German Wikipedia names the Institut auf dem Rosenberg); exact dates and duties are not consistently reported. Month defaulted
stops.campa: He tries the German-speaking world once more, teaching at the Institut auf dem Rosenberg above St Gallen, a boarding school for the children of the rich. It lasts about a year and does not hold him. Switzerland offers him a comfortable post and he finds he cannot breathe in it; England offers provincial obscurity and he goes back to it on purpose. From here the arrangement holds. He keeps the language and declines the country, and he never states this anywhere as a position.
suggested_refs: The Institut auf dem Rosenberg, St Gallen, Sebald's brief Swiss school post

stops.name: Norwich, the University of East Anglia
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month not recorded and defaulted
stops.campa: Sebald joins the University of East Anglia as a lecturer in German and stays thirty-one years. The campus is new concrete laid on farmland outside Norwich, in a county the trains end at and travellers pass through only if they mean to. Flat fields, round church towers, a coastline that gives ground to the sea every winter. He will take a chair here, found an institute, and write five books from this county. He never moves to a city where any of them are discussed.
suggested_refs: The University of East Anglia, Norwich, Sebald's institution from 1970 to his death

stops.name: Norwich, the doctorate on Döblin
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the degree; month not recorded and defaulted
stops.campa: Sebald takes his doctorate at East Anglia with a thesis on Alfred Döblin, the Berlin novelist who fled in 1933 and came back after the war to find no readers waiting for him. The subject is a German writer made foreign by history, examined by a German who has made himself foreign deliberately. He goes on producing academic criticism for another fifteen years, sharp and quarrelsome about Austrian and German authors, and tells nobody that the work he means to do has not begun.
suggested_refs: 'The Revival of Myth: A Study of Alfred Döblin's Novels', UEA doctoral thesis, 1973

stops.name: Wymondham, the first Norfolk house
stops.date_confidence: residence in Wymondham is attested but the years are not fixed in reachable sources; the date is set at a mid-decade point within the attested period and should be read as approximate
stops.campa: He settles his family west of Norwich: his Austrian wife Ute, their daughter Anna, an old house in a market town with an abbey too large for it. He gardens, drives the lanes, walks. The county keeps its ruins in plain view and declines to explain them either, but this is a silence he can live inside, because it is not his family's. Being permanently and slightly foreign becomes the condition he writes from, and he arranges the rest of his life so as to remain in it.
suggested_refs: Wymondham Abbey and the Sebald household in the Norfolk market town

stops.name: Hamburg, the habilitation taken when he least needs it
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month not recorded and defaulted. Coordinates corrected to the university main building on Edmund-Siemers-Allee, replacing a figure in the research pool that fell some 800 m west in the Karolinenviertel
stops.campa: Sebald submits his habilitation at the University of Hamburg, the qualification that would have opened a German professorial career had he wanted one. He is forty-two, has lived in England twenty years, and collects the German credential at the moment he has least use for it. Two years later he publishes a long poem instead. The scholar's apparatus stays with him. He goes on visiting archives and producing photographs as evidence, and he carries the habit into books that are not scholarship and are not quite fiction.
suggested_refs: The Universität Hamburg, where Sebald habilitated in 1986

stops.name: Poringland, the village and After Nature
stops.date_confidence: publication of Nach der Natur attested to 1988, month not recorded and defaulted; the Poringland residence is attested but its start year is not. Coordinates corrected to the village proper, replacing a research-pool figure some 1.7 km to the north-east
stops.campa: From the village of Poringland, south of Norwich, Sebald publishes Nach der Natur, a long poem in three parts: the painter Matthias Grünewald, the naturalist Georg Wilhelm Steller on Bering's voyage to the Arctic, and his own family, the bombing raids, the Allgäu childhood. He is forty-four and has published nothing until now but criticism. The three lives run in parallel and none of them ends well; the wrecking of nature and the wrecking of people are set down in one register, without a seam.
suggested_refs: Nach der Natur: Ein Elementargedicht (1988), Sebald's first literary book

stops.name: Norwich, the British Centre for Literary Translation
stops.date_confidence: founding attested to 1989, month defaulted; the chair of European literature is dated 1987 in the research pool but tagged there as reconstruction, so that year is carried here as reported rather than as fixed
stops.campa: Sebald founds the British Centre for Literary Translation at East Anglia, two years after being given the chair of European literature. The institute exists because he holds that a book has to be able to cross a border, having crossed one himself and gone on writing in the language he left on the far side. His translators, Michael Hulse and afterwards Anthea Bell, work with him line by line and are argued with line by line. He publishes in German and is read in English, and he stays in the gap on purpose.
suggested_refs: The British Centre for Literary Translation, UEA, founded by Sebald in 1989

stops.name: Vienna, the walking that will not stop
stops.date_confidence: the research pool dates the episode c. 1980 as narrated in the 1990 book; Sebald's own travel is not separately documented, and month and day are defaulted
stops.campa: In the book that becomes Schwindel. Gefühle the narrator reaches Vienna and walks. He walks until his shoes come apart, hours a day, over streets whose limits he afterwards traces on a map and finds shaped like a closed circuit he could not get out of. He visits the poet Ernst Herbeck at the asylum and takes him out for a day in the country. In a crowd he believes he sees Dante, banished from his own city and dead six hundred years. Too many of the dead are abroad at once, and that is what the title of the book means.
suggested_refs: Ernst Herbeck, the asylum poet visited in the 'All'estero' section of Vertigo

stops.name: Venice, reading himself into other travellers
stops.date_confidence: narrative date only, c. 1980, as recounted in the 1990 book; no independent travel record. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He goes south to Venice and finds the city already occupied by other men's texts: Casanova counting the days of his imprisonment under the leads of the Doge's palace, Grillparzer visiting the same cell and disliking it, Kafka arriving in 1913 too ill to enjoy anything at all. The narrator reads himself into every one of them. He sits in a cafe, takes the boat, and cannot establish whether the streets are repeating or he is. The city stands on piles that are quietly rotting underneath it.
suggested_refs: Casanova's cell under the Piombi, revisited in Vertigo

stops.name: Verona, the name on the pizzeria licence
stops.date_confidence: narrative date only, c. 1980, as recounted in the 1990 book. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: In Verona the narrator eats at the Pizzeria Verona, reads the proprietor's name on the licence, Carlo Cadavero, and leaves the city that night in something close to panic. The Giardino Giusti gives him no rest either. Years afterwards he returns to look for the restaurant and finds it shut and its papers gone. Kafka's hunter Gracchus, the dead man whose funeral boat never makes land, is at work in the book around him, and the narrator has begun to suspect the pattern is not literary but personal.
suggested_refs: The Pizzeria Verona and the Giardino Giusti, sites of the Verona episode in Vertigo

stops.name: Riva del Garda, Dr K takes the waters
stops.date_confidence: narrative date only; the Riva section retells Kafka's documented stay of September 1913, while the narrator's own visit is undated in the book. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The book follows Kafka to Riva del Garda, where in September 1913 the Prague insurance official took a sanatorium cure, rowed on the lake, and conducted an attachment to a Swiss girl he recorded and never named. Sebald retells the trip in the third person as Dr K. Here too is the bark of the huntsman Gracchus, carrying a man with a wound that will not close and no harbour willing to admit him. The cure becomes a template. A man falls ill and travels, because staying where he is has become impossible.
suggested_refs: Kafka's September 1913 sanatorium stay at Riva, retold as 'Dr K Takes the Waters at Riva'

stops.name: Wertach im Allgäu, the return to W.
stops.date_confidence: narrative date c. 1987 as given in the research pool for the closing section of the 1990 book; not independently documented. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The last part of the book brings the narrator back to W., which is Wertach with one letter left of it, after thirty years away. He takes a room at the inn, walks the village, and finds it rebuilt nearly past recognition while the arrangement underneath stands intact. The people who were adults in his childhood are old or dead, and still nothing is said. He inventories rooms, furniture, a painter's studio, a hunter found dead in the snow. Going home produces no reconciliation. It produces an inventory.
stops.quote: Going home is not necessarily a wonderful experience. It always comes with a sense of loss and makes you so conscious of the inexorable passage of time.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Sebald on quotation aggregators; primary interview not traced [R]
suggested_refs: 'Il ritorno in patria', the closing section of Vertigo, set in the village of W.

segments.name: An English Pilgrimage: the Suffolk Coast, August 1992

stops.name: Somerleyton Hall, the contractor's fortune and its collapse
stops.date_confidence: the walk is dated by the book's opening sentence to August 1992; the day of each halt is not given and defaults to the first
stops.campa: In August 1992, as the dog days end, Sebald sets out on foot down the Suffolk coast. His first halt is Somerleyton Hall, built by Sir Morton Peto, the railway contractor who raised Nelson's Column and the Reform Club and then went bankrupt for millions. The glass winter gardens are gone, the ballroom smells of dust, a miniature railway runs where the money used to be. From the first day the walk has its subject: a splendour put up fast on nothing, already half returned to the ground.
suggested_refs: Somerleyton Hall and the bankruptcy of Sir Samuel Morton Peto
sources: W.G. Sebald, Die Ringe des Saturn (1995) / The Rings of Saturn (1998)

stops.name: Lowestoft, the herring port with the fleet gone
stops.date_confidence: August 1992 per the book; exact day not given and defaulted
stops.campa: He walks into Lowestoft, once the busiest herring port on the coast, with a fleet that took fish out of the North Sea in millions and a promenade of hotels for the visitors who came to watch it land. The fleet is gone. He takes a room at a decayed hotel, eats a piece of grey fish alone in the dining room, and counts boarded frontages on the way back. Nothing has destroyed this town. It has simply been left, and the leaving has been more thorough than any bombardment he writes about.
suggested_refs: The Lowestoft herring fishery and its collapse, treated at length in The Rings of Saturn
sources: W.G. Sebald, The Rings of Saturn (1995/1998)

stops.name: Benacre Broad, the coast the sea is taking
stops.date_confidence: August 1992 per the book; day defaulted. Coordinates corrected eastward to the coastal lagoon, replacing a research-pool longitude that fell some 4 km inland near Wrentham
stops.campa: Beyond the town the path runs along a cliff of soft sand the sea takes at a yard or two a year. At Benacre Broad the freshwater lagoon lies behind a shingle bar with dead trees standing in it where the salt has come through, and the whole arrangement will be gone inside a lifetime. Sebald lies down in the sand and dreams of a drowned coast. The North Sea is doing here, in slow motion, what fire did to the German cities in a night, and nobody along this shore calls it a catastrophe.
suggested_refs: Benacre Broad and the eroding Suffolk cliffs between Kessingland and Covehithe
sources: W.G. Sebald, The Rings of Saturn (1995/1998)

stops.name: Covehithe, the small church inside the ruined one
stops.date_confidence: August 1992 per the book; day defaulted. Coordinates corrected to the village, replacing a research-pool figure some 2 km inland to the south-west
stops.campa: At Covehithe there is almost no parish left. The great medieval church of St Andrew, always too large for the place, was pulled down by its own parishioners in the seventeenth century; they left the tall tower standing and put up a small thatched church among the ruins in 1672, so that one building now sits inside the shell of another. Sebald walks the field edge to the cliff and looks down at where the rest of the village used to be. The road that once ran on north ends in air.
suggested_refs: St Andrew's, Covehithe: the 1672 thatched church built within the medieval ruin
sources: W.G. Sebald, The Rings of Saturn (1995/1998)

stops.name: Southwold, the earth turning into the dark
stops.date_confidence: August 1992 per the book; day defaulted
stops.campa: He comes into Southwold in the evening and lies on the cliff above the beach as the light goes. Offshore, on a day in 1672, the Dutch and English fleets fought the battle of Sole Bay within sight of the town; the noise carried inland for hours and the dead washed up for weeks. None of it shows. He reads Thomas Browne on the huntsmen already up in America while men in Persia are past their first sleep, and watches the shadow of the night cross the water at a speed a man can see.
stops.quote: As I sat there in Southwold overlooking the German Ocean, I sensed quite clearly the earth's slow turning into the dark.
stops.quote_source: The Rings of Saturn, trans. Michael Hulse (1998), p. 78
suggested_refs: The battle of Sole Bay, 1672, fought offshore from Southwold
sources: W.G. Sebald, The Rings of Saturn (1995/1998)

stops.name: Dunwich, the city under the water
stops.date_confidence: August 1992 per the book; day defaulted
stops.campa: Dunwich was a city: a bishop's seat, parish churches by the handful, a fleet, gates, a mint. The sea took it street by street across four centuries and the last church went over the cliff within living memory. Above the waterline there remain heath, a fragment of the Greyfriars wall, and gravestones at the edge of the drop. Sebald walks the heath, loses his direction among paths that keep turning back, and comes out where he went in. The archive here is offshore, under grey water.
stops.quote: Places seem to me to have some kind of memory, in that they activate memory in those who look at them.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Sebald on quotation aggregators; primary interview not traced [R]
suggested_refs: The lost port of Dunwich and the Greyfriars ruin above the cliff
sources: W.G. Sebald, The Rings of Saturn (1995/1998)

stops.name: Middleton, the visit to Michael Hamburger
stops.date_confidence: August 1992 per the book's own dating of the walk; the research pool wrongly attached this encounter to the 1995 publication year, and that error is corrected here. Day defaulted
stops.campa: Inland at Middleton he calls on Michael Hamburger, poet and translator, taken out of Berlin as a boy in 1933 and English ever since. They walk the garden and the house. Hamburger keeps his study as though the arrangement of pencils on the desk could be carried across from somewhere else; Sebald, writing it down, can no longer establish which of the two of them is remembering the Berlin flat. Two German-born writers in an English county, one of whom will render the other's last poems into English.
suggested_refs: Michael Hamburger's house and garden at Middleton, Suffolk
sources: W.G. Sebald, The Rings of Saturn (1995/1998)

stops.name: Orford Ness, the catastrophe held in reserve
stops.date_confidence: August 1992 per the book; day defaulted
stops.campa: He crosses to Orford Ness, a shingle spit the Ministry of Defence held for most of the century and told nobody about. Radar was worked out on this ground; here the detonators of atomic weapons were tested in concrete chambers roofed to lift and vent an accident upward. The pagodas stand empty on the stones and parts of the spit remain marked out of bounds. At Dunwich a catastrophe happened slowly and can be visited. On the Ness a catastrophe was prepared, kept ready, and never used.
suggested_refs: The Atomic Weapons Research Establishment test pagodas on Orford Ness
sources: W.G. Sebald, The Rings of Saturn (1995/1998)

stops.name: Boulge, the rose on FitzGerald's grave
stops.date_confidence: August 1992 per the book; day defaulted. The research pool called the plant a mulberry, which is wrong and appears to have bled in from the book's silk material; the rose provenance is corrected here from the Edward FitzGerald article
stops.campa: In the churchyard of St Michael's, Boulge, he finds the grave of Edward FitzGerald, who lived nearby with almost no external event in his life and made the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam out of a Persian manuscript and a great deal of licence. On the grave grows a rose: hips gathered at Khayyam's tomb at Nishapur in 1886, raised at Kew, a cutting set here. A plant carried four thousand miles to root over a translator. Sebald, writing in one language to be read in another, notes it and walks on.
suggested_refs: The Khayyam rose on Edward FitzGerald's grave, St Michael's, Boulge
sources: W.G. Sebald, The Rings of Saturn (1995/1998)

stops.name: Ditchingham, Rider Haggard's two books
stops.date_confidence: August 1992 per the book; day defaulted. Location uncertain: Rider Haggard lived at Ditchingham House, his wife's family seat, not at Ditchingham Hall, the Earls Ferrers' house that the research pool named; the coordinates given here correspond cleanly to neither and should be read as the estate area
stops.campa: North of the Waveney he passes the Ditchingham estate, where Henry Rider Haggard wrote King Solomon's Mines and She and, in old age, a survey of English agriculture that reads as a record of collapse: farms let go, labourers drawn off to the towns, fields returning to scrub. The man who invented a lost African kingdom spent his last working years documenting a real one at his own gate. Sebald reads the two books as a single book. The route bends homeward now, through country as emptied as the coast.
suggested_refs: Ditchingham House, Norfolk, home of H. Rider Haggard; his Rural England survey
sources: W.G. Sebald, The Rings of Saturn (1995/1998)

stops.name: Bungay, the circuit closed on silk
stops.date_confidence: August 1992 per the book; day defaulted
stops.campa: The circuit closes near Bungay, and Sebald walks the last miles in a condition he describes as barely able to continue. The book does not end at the sea. It ends in mulberry leaves, in silkworms, in the sericulture schemes of Chinese empresses and Prussian kings, and at last in the silk programme taught in German schools under the Reich, where the killing of the worms in their cocoons was set out for children as a lesson in hygiene. The thread runs from a Suffolk lane to a classroom in the Allgäu.
suggested_refs: The sericulture chapters that close The Rings of Saturn
sources: W.G. Sebald, The Rings of Saturn (1995/1998)

segments.name: The Emigrants, the Rings, and the Air War

stops.name: Manchester, the emigrant's city written back
stops.date_confidence: publication of Die Ausgewanderten attested to 1992; month not recorded and defaulted. The stop is placed at Manchester, the setting of the book's fourth narrative, rather than at the publisher's city
stops.campa: Die Ausgewanderten appears: four lives, a schoolteacher, a doctor, a great-uncle, a painter, each driven out of Germany or into a private exile, each ending in suicide or in something adjacent to it. The painter Max Ferber works in a Manchester studio where the dust of decades is left where it falls, and the city Sebald taught in at twenty-two comes back as the terminus of a German-Jewish life. Small blurred photographs sit in the text uncaptioned. Readers write in to ask whether the people are real.
suggested_refs: Die Ausgewanderten (1992), trans. Michael Hulse as The Emigrants (1996)

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, Eichborn publishes the Rings
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested; month not recorded and defaulted. Coordinates are the publisher's city, Frankfurt am Main, not a specific building
stops.campa: Eichborn of Frankfurt publishes Die Ringe des Saturn, subtitled Eine englische Wallfahrt, an English pilgrimage. Three hundred and seventy pages, a walk of about a week, and inside it Thomas Browne's missing skull, the herring fishery, the Taiping rebellion, Roger Casement in the Congo, the sugar money behind the Suffolk gentry, and the burning of the German cities. The photographs are grey, small and unlabelled. The frame is a man in a Norwich hospital bed a year after the walk, unable to move, writing it down.
suggested_refs: Die Ringe des Saturn: Eine englische Wallfahrt, Eichborn Verlag, 1995

stops.name: Zurich, the lectures on the air war
stops.date_confidence: attested to late autumn 1997 (de.wikipedia: 'im Spätherbst 1997 im Zürcher Puppentheater'); the day is not recorded and defaults to the first of November
stops.campa: In late autumn Sebald gives a course of lectures in a Zurich puppet theatre on the Allied bombing of Germany and its near-total absence from German literature. Hundreds of thousands of civilians dead, scores of cities burnt out, and a national literature that went around the subject. He is accused of tactlessness, of ingratitude, of pressing the wrong case at the wrong hour. Letters arrive for years afterwards from people who were in the cellars as children and had never once been asked.
stops.quote: I see the catastrophe caused by the Germans, dreadful as it was, by no means as a singular event – it developed with a certain logic from European history and then, for the same reason, ate itself into European history.
stops.quote_source: Interview quotation as reproduced in the English Wikipedia article 'W. G. Sebald'; primary interview and date not traced
suggested_refs: Luftkrieg und Literatur (Carl Hanser, 1999), from the Zurich lectures of 1997

stops.name: London, the Rings of Saturn in English
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested; month not recorded and defaulted. Coordinates are the standard atlas pin for London, since the book was issued jointly in London and New York
stops.campa: Michael Hulse's translation of The Rings of Saturn is published in London and New York, and Sebald arrives in English as a writer with no shelf to stand on: a German professor at a provincial English university producing walking books full of photographs nobody can classify. Reviewers reach for the word hybrid. The books sell steadily and then quickly. Within three years he is discussed as a candidate for the Nobel Prize, in a country where he has taught quietly for twenty-eight years.
stops.quote: A hybrid of a book – fiction, travel, biography, myth, and memoir
stops.quote_source: Roberta Silman, review of The Rings of Saturn, The New York Times, 1998
suggested_refs: The Rings of Saturn, trans. Michael Hulse, Harvill / New Directions, 1998

stops.name: Antwerp Centraal, the stranger in the waiting room
stops.date_confidence: the novel dates the first meeting to the 1960s; Sebald's own research travel for the book falls in the later 1990s and is not individually documented, so this and the following stops are placed in that research period with month and day defaulted [R]
stops.campa: The novel that becomes Austerlitz opens in the vaulted hall of Antwerp Centraal, a station built with Congo money in the shape of a cathedral, where a stranger with a rucksack is photographing the roof. He explains the building to the narrator, who has asked nothing of him. Over thirty years the two meet by accident in waiting rooms and station bars, and the stranger gives out his life in fragments, working inward from architecture: fortresses, termini, the nineteenth century's buildings for outlasting their contents.
suggested_refs: Antwerpen-Centraal station, the opening setting of Austerlitz

stops.name: Liverpool Street Station, the room being demolished
stops.date_confidence: novel setting; the recovered arrival is dated 1939 within the fiction, while Sebald's own visits to the station fall during its 1990s rebuilding. Month and day defaulted [R]
stops.campa: In the disused Ladies' Waiting Room at Liverpool Street Station, among the demolition works, Austerlitz recovers what he has spent fifty years not knowing: that he came into this station in the summer of 1939 on a train out of Prague, four and a half years old, with a small rucksack and a label, and was collected by a Welsh minister who gave him another name and forbade the first. Sebald walks the station while it is being rebuilt. The room the book requires is being taken out as he writes it.
suggested_refs: The Kindertransport arrivals at Liverpool Street Station, 1938-1939

stops.name: Prague, the neighbour who remembers him at four
stops.date_confidence: novel setting, undated within the fiction; placed in Sebald's research years of the later 1990s, month and day defaulted [R]
stops.campa: Austerlitz returns to Prague and finds the street, the house, the flat, and Vera, his mother's neighbour, who has been there the whole time and remembers him at four years old. Czech comes back to him in her hallway, entire, a language he did not know he still had. Of his mother Agata, an opera singer, there survive a photograph, a theatre programme, and a date of transport. Sebald builds the search out of real archives, hands it to a man who does not exist, and prints the photographs.
suggested_refs: The Prague archives and the Kindertransport records used in Austerlitz

stops.name: Terezín, the locked town
stops.date_confidence: novel setting, undated within the fiction; placed in Sebald's research years, month and day defaulted [R]
stops.campa: He goes to Terezin, the garrison town the Reich ran as a ghetto and showed to the Red Cross with the shopfronts repainted. The streets are empty when Austerlitz walks them, every door locked, the museum shut for the season; through the windows he can make out nothing but his own reflection lying over the goods inside. The propaganda film shot there in 1944 he slows to a quarter speed, looking for one face. His mother was held in this town and sent east. The record ends at a transport list.
stops.quote: The moral backbone of literature is about that whole question of memory.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Sebald on quotation aggregators; primary interview not traced [R]
suggested_refs: The 1944 Theresienstadt propaganda film, slowed and searched in Austerlitz

stops.name: Paris, the library over the warehouse
stops.date_confidence: novel setting, undated within the fiction; placed in the research years, month and day defaulted [R]. Coordinates are the canonical atlas pin for Paris, inherited unchanged; the Bibliothèque nationale site at Tolbiac actually lies at about 48.8355, 2.3765, and the two are deliberately not merged
stops.campa: In Paris, Austerlitz searches the archives for his father and works in the new national library on the Quai de la Gare, four glass towers built in the shape of open books with the readers put underground. An attendant tells him what stood on the site: a warehouse where everything taken from the flats of Parisian Jews was sorted, catalogued and shipped away, furniture, linen, spoons, pianos, a whole city's household goods. The new building stands on it. Sebald sets the fact down and draws no conclusion from it.
suggested_refs: The Bibliothèque nationale de France at Tolbiac and the Austerlitz-Tolbiac warehouse of looted Jewish property

stops.name: Munich, Carl Hanser publishes Austerlitz
stops.date_confidence: the research pool gives 2001-11-06 for the German publication; the English translation by Anthea Bell appeared the same year. Coordinates are the publisher's city, not a specific building
stops.campa: Carl Hanser of Munich publishes Austerlitz, and Anthea Bell's English version appears the same year. Sentences run for pages, there are no chapter breaks, and the photographs are pressed into the text like exhibits in a case nobody is prosecuting. The reviews are the best of his life. He is fifty-seven, widely read at last, and spends the autumn on trains and in radio studios across western Europe giving interviews in two languages about a book concerned with the impossibility of recovering anything.
stops.quote_source: James Wood, on the uncaptioned photographs in Austerlitz, quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Austerlitz (novel)'
suggested_refs: Austerlitz, Carl Hanser Verlag, 2001; trans. Anthea Bell, Independent Foreign Fiction Prize 2002

stops.name: Near Poringland, the heart stops at the wheel
stops.date_confidence: date attested; location approximate. No consulted source fixes the road or milepost, and the sources conflict: the research pool offered two different points inside or west of Norwich, while German Wikipedia places the crash near his home at Poringland. The coordinates here are the Poringland area, not a located crash site
stops.campa: On a Friday in December Sebald drives out with his daughter Anna beside him. On the road his heart fails, the car crosses into the path of an oncoming lorry, and he is killed at once. Anna survives. He is fifty-seven. He had known for years that he had a cardiac insufficiency, and had written to a correspondent that June that he was condemned to unrest. The coroner's report comes six months later and finds that the heart attack came first and caused the collision, which reverses the order every early account had given.
stops.quote: Condemned to unrest I am, I am afraid
stops.quote_source: Letter to Andreas Dorschel, June 2001, quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'W. G. Sebald'
suggested_refs: The coroner's report on Sebald's death, issued mid-2002

stops.name: Framingham Earl, the grave at St Andrew's
stops.date_confidence: burial attested to December 2001; the day is not recorded and defaults to the first. Coordinates follow the afterlife lens, which the research pool itself judged closer to correct than its own geography figure some 1.4 km to the north-west
stops.campa: He is buried in the churchyard of St Andrew's at Framingham Earl, a small round-towered Norfolk church a few fields from the village he lived in, in a country he chose at twenty-two and never claimed as his own. The grave is plain. Norwich, where he taught for thirty-one years, is a few miles up the road; Wertach is seven hundred miles the other way, and the Allgäu had no hold on him by then. In August he had told a visitor, without dramatising it, what he thought was coming.
stops.quote: someone who knows he has to leave before too long
stops.quote_source: Reported statement to a visitor, August 2001, quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'W. G. Sebald'
suggested_refs: St Andrew's churchyard, Framingham Earl, Norfolk

stops.name: Norwich, the beech and the bench at Sebald Copse
stops.date_confidence: planting attested to 2003; month not recorded and defaulted
stops.campa: His family plants a copper beech on the campus at East Anglia and sets a round wooden bench about it, the circle taken from the shape of the Suffolk walk. Cut into the wood is a line from the penultimate poem of Unerzählt, the book he made with the painter Jan Peter Tripp and did not live to see: unrecounted always it will remain, the story of the averted faces. The English is Michael Hamburger's, whom he walked inland to visit at Middleton. Students sit on it without knowing whose it is.
stops.quote: Unerzählt bleibt die Geschichte der abgewandten Gesichter
stops.quote_source: Inscription on the memorial bench at Sebald Copse, University of East Anglia, from the penultimate poem of Unerzählt (2003); English rendering by Michael Hamburger, cited in Catling and Hibbitt, eds., Saturn's Moons (2011), p. 659
suggested_refs: Sebald Copse and its inscribed circular bench, University of East Anglia

stops.name: Wertach im Allgäu, the path that ends at the birth house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of opening, 13 November 2005
stops.campa: A marked path opens in the Allgäu: about twelve kilometres from Oberjoch down to Wertach, six steles along the way carrying passages from Schwindel. Gefühle, and at the end of it the house on the Grüntenseestrasse where he was born. Walkers come from England and Japan to do it in a day. The village that agreed for sixty years to describe nothing has set his sentences on posts in its own fields, and walking, which was his method and half his subject, is now the way people arrive here.
suggested_refs: The Sebaldweg, Oberjoch to Wertach, opened 13 November 2005
